reference.title: Lying Leg Raise and Hold
reference.listing: Page could not be read (gymvisual.com is blocked by the network proxy); movement taken from the exercise name and standard coaching practice

breathing.pattern: Exhale as the legs rise; keep breathing slowly and shallowly through the hold (do not hold the breath); inhale as they lower.
breathing.cadence: About 1.2 s up, 3 s hold, 2 s down

prescription.reps: 5-8 holds of 3-5 s (or one 15-30 s hold)
prescription.tempo: About 1.2 s up, 3-5 s hold, 2 s down
prescription.progression: Longer holds, then lower holds (30 degrees), then add slow flutters during the hold

cues.text: Lie flat, arms by your sides palms down, legs straight and together, heels just off the mat.
Breathe out and lift both legs together to about 45 degrees, knees long.
Hold still. Low back pressed into the mat, ribs down, keep breathing.
Lower slowly, stopping with the heels just above the floor.

mistakes.mistake: Low back arching off the mat during the hold
mistakes.fix: Raise the legs higher or bend the knees until the back stays flat.
Breathe slowly through the hold while keeping the brace.

mistakes.mistake: Legs drifting down or shaking apart
mistakes.fix: Squeeze the legs together and pick a shorter hold you can keep still.

mistakes.mistake: Pushing hard into the floor with the hands and neck
mistakes.fix: Hands rest lightly; head relaxed on the mat.

kinematics.norm: Held at about 45 degrees; lower holds are harder (clinical opinion)
About 45 degrees during the hold (clinical opinion)
Pelvis stays on the mat; the low back should not arch (clinical opinion; McGill 1998 for the load)
Controlled lift, 3-5 s still hold, slow lowering (clinical opinion)

sources.title: GymVisual #5109, Lying Leg Raise and Hold, video (movement reference; page not readable here)

McGill 1998, low back exercises: evidence for improving exercise regimens (Phys Ther 78(7):754-765; PMID 9672547)

cautions: Stop if you feel sharp, radiating or nerve-type pain.
Muscle glow colours and activation curves are illustrative, not measured EMG.

Straight-leg raises load the low back: leg raises gave higher psoas activity and spine compression than sit-ups in McGill's data (McGill 1998). If the low back arches off the mat, bend the knees or shorten the range.
Low-back pain or disc problems: prefer bent-knee raises, dead bugs or curl-ups.
Pregnancy and postpartum (diastasis recti): get individual guidance before dynamic trunk-flexion or straight-leg work.
modify: Bend the knees to shorten the lever.
Hands under the hips if the low back lifts.
Shorter range: stop lowering higher up.
regressions: Single-leg hold with the other foot on the floor.
progressions: Small flutter kicks during the hold.

muscleNotes.hip_flexors_r: Iliopsoas lifts and lowers the legs. Bilateral leg lifts gave higher iliacus activity than hip-flexion sit-ups (Andersson 1997), and leg raises produced the highest psoas activity in McGill's comparison (McGill 1998).
muscleNotes.hip_flexors_l: Iliopsoas lifts and lowers the legs. Bilateral leg lifts gave higher iliacus activity than hip-flexion sit-ups (Andersson 1997), and leg raises produced the highest psoas activity in McGill's comparison (McGill 1998).
muscleNotes.core: Rectus abdominis does not move the legs; it holds the pelvis and low back against the pull of the hip flexors. Bilateral, but not unilateral, leg lifts needed abdominal activation (Andersson 1997). Leg lowering gave less rectus activity than curl-ups (Clark 2003).
muscleNotes.obliques_r: Brace with the rectus to stop the low back arching.
muscleNotes.obliques_l: Brace with the rectus to stop the low back arching.
muscleNotes.adductors_r: Keep the legs together and assist hip flexion near the bottom (clinical opinion).
muscleNotes.adductors_l: Keep the legs together and assist hip flexion near the bottom (clinical opinion).
muscleNotes.quads_r: Keep the knees straight; rectus femoris also helps flex the hips.
muscleNotes.quads_l: Keep the knees straight; rectus femoris also helps flex the hips.
